source: Trading in the Zone - Mark Douglas (concept)
text: A loss is a normal business expense of trading, not a personal insult. Each trade is independent; the market owes you nothing. Trying to 'win it back' turns the next trade into an emotional decision instead of a probabilistic one.

source: The Daily Trading Coach - Brett Steenbarger (concept)
text: Use a mandatory cool-down rule: after a losing trade, step away from the screen for a fixed time (for example 20-30 minutes) and write down what happened before you are allowed to place the next order.

source: Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom - Van K. Tharp (concept)
text: Position size is decided by a fixed rule (e.g., risk 1% of capital per trade), never by how you feel. Increasing size after a loss is the fastest path to a large drawdown.

source: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator - Edwin Lefevre (concept)
text: Money is made by waiting for the right setup, not by constant activity. Set a maximum number of trades per day and treat unused trade slots as a sign of discipline, not missed opportunity.

source: The Disciplined Trader - Mark Douglas (concept)
text: Write a trading plan that defines exactly which setups you trade, your entry, stop-loss and target. Any trade that does not match the plan is not taken, no matter how tempting.

source: Trading in the Zone - Mark Douglas (concept)
text: There is always another opportunity. Chasing a stock after a large move with a volume spike usually means buying from those who entered earlier. Wait for a pullback or a fresh setup that matches your plan.

source: Thinking, Fast and Slow - Daniel Kahneman (concept)
text: Fast, intuitive thinking reacts to vivid recent price moves. Slow the decision down with a pre-trade checklist so the analytical system gets a chance to check the setup.

source: The Psychology of Trading - Brett Steenbarger (concept)
text: Fear spikes during sharp, high-volume moves. Decide your exit (stop-loss) before entering, so you do not need to make exit decisions while emotionally flooded. Use slow breathing and a short pause before any unplanned exit.

source: Trading for a Living - Alexander Elder (concept)
text: Your stop-loss already defines the maximum you accept to lose. Exiting earlier out of fear cuts trades that would have worked and destroys the edge of the system.

source: Thinking, Fast and Slow - Daniel Kahneman (concept)
text: People feel losses roughly twice as strongly as equal gains, which makes them hold losers hoping to break even. Recognise that 'hoping' is the signal to exit.

source: Trading for a Living - Alexander Elder (concept)
text: Never average down on a losing position. Cut losses short, let profits run. Review every loss that exceeded 1R and ask what rule was broken.

source: Trading for a Living - Alexander Elder (concept)
text: Place the stop-loss order in the system the moment you enter, and only ever move it in the direction of your trade (to lock in profit), never further away.

source: Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom - Van K. Tharp (concept)
text: Think in R-multiples. Define the target before entry; book at least partial profit at target and trail the stop for the rest, instead of giving back an open gain.

source: Market Wizards - Jack Schwager (concept)
text: Successful traders repeatedly emphasise survival over maximum gain. Excessive leverage turns a normal losing streak into an account-ending event.

source: Trading for a Living - Alexander Elder (concept)
text: Use the 2% rule (never risk more than 2% of equity on one trade) and the 6% rule (stop trading for the month if total losses reach 6% of equity).

source: Thinking, Fast and Slow - Daniel Kahneman (concept)
text: Before entering, write one clear reason the trade could fail and the price level that proves you wrong. Actively look at indicators that disagree with your view.

source: The Black Swan - Nassim Taleb (concept)
text: Seeking only confirming evidence creates false confidence. Treat contrary signals (opposite MACD, negative sentiment) as data, not noise.

source: Atomic Habits - James Clear (concept)
text: Make good behaviour easy and obvious: a printed pre-trade checklist next to the screen, a fixed trading window, and a daily review habit tied to market close.

source: The Daily Trading Coach - Brett Steenbarger (concept)
text: Keep a trading journal: setup, reason, emotion before entry, outcome, and lesson. Review it weekly to find the one repeated mistake to fix next week.

source: Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom - Van K. Tharp (concept)
text: A strategy can only be judged over a large sample of trades (e.g., 30+). Switching strategies after a few losses means you never learn whether any strategy has an edge.

source: Trading in the Zone - Mark Douglas (concept)
text: Consistency comes from accepting risk fully before each trade. When the risk is accepted in advance, the outcome no longer triggers fear or euphoria.

source: Market Wizards - Jack Schwager (concept)
text: Keep risk per trade constant. A consistent size makes results measurable and stops one emotional trade from erasing weeks of progress.
